note: Evidence for flag eras. An era is listed only once someone has read its sources; every other era is unreviewed. Only positive evidence is written here, and what could not be confirmed is said in `open`, not left out.

classes.attested: Sources show this flag in use in this period. Needs one primary or reference source, or two compiled sources from different publishers.
classes.reconstructed: Described in sources but no image survives; the drawing is a reconstruction.
classes.symbolic: An emblem, banner or standard shown for a polity that had no flag of its own.
classes.none: No flag evidence exists; the image is a placeholder.
classes.unreviewed: Not yet checked against sources. The page text is the original compilation.

kinds.primary: The decree, document, image or object itself, or a museum record of it.
kinds.reference: A scholarly or institutional account that names its basis.
kinds.compiled: A general compilation (Wikipedia, Flags of the World); useful, but a copy of other writers.

nos-1944.title: 5e Koninginnedag in onderdrukking: geen vlaggen, geen oranje (31 August 1944)
nos-1944.note: A broadcaster's retrospective of 1944 news. It says that since 1940 any demonstrative act for the House of Orange was punishable; it does not say what happened to the tricolour.

era-1945.says: A royal decree of 19 February 1937, no. 93, fixed the colours of the flag of the Kingdom as red, white and blue; FOTW and Wikipedia both quote it that way. The Royal House says the colours were bright vermilion and cobalt blue.
era-1945.open: The sources disagree on the shade: FOTW dates 'bright vermilion and cobalt blue' to 1958, while the Royal House page gives that wording as the decree's own. The decree text itself has not been read. The hex swatches on this page are approximations, not a specification.

era-1940.says: FOTW, citing Poels in Vexilla Nostra 198 (1995), says the tricolour stayed the national flag but its use was restricted by the occupiers. NOS reports that from 1940 any demonstrative act for the House of Orange was punishable.
era-1940.open: No ordinance was found, so which restrictions fell on the tricolour, and when, is not established. An earlier version of this page said it was 'banned outright in 1943'; no source for that was found and it was removed. The flag drawn is the occupier's, schematically.

era-1830.open: Not yet checked against a source. That the flag was unchanged through the 1830 secession is plausible but unsourced here.

era-1813.says: Wikipedia reports 1813 newspapers describing red-white-blue flags with orange pennants and solid orange flags, and says the question of the national flag was left undecided; its statement that William preferred red-white-blue is marked 'citation needed' there. The Royal House confirms independence returned in 1813 but says nothing about the flag.
era-1813.open: One secondary source for the flag question; not enough to call it attested.

era-1810.says: The Royal House says the Netherlands was annexed by France in 1810 and the national flag was replaced by the French imperial standard. Wikipedia says the national flag was replaced by imperial emblems in 1810, without a citation there.
era-1810.open: Which French flag flew on Dutch buildings is not established; 'imperial standard' may not be the plain tricolour drawn here. Wikipedia's own Kingdom of Holland page gives the annexation date inconsistently.

era-1806.says: The tricolour continued under Louis Bonaparte. Wikipedia dates the flag without the Maiden to 5 June 1806 (no citation there), records naval crews rioting over the flag in August 1806 and a royal decree of 1 December 1807 affirming the Statenvlag for the navy (both citing de Jonge, 1831). FOTW says Louis proposed adding quartered arms to the navy's flag and withdrew the proposal when the navy would not accept it.
era-1806.open: The 5 June 1806 date has no primary source behind it in either reference. The motive this page used to state ('a deliberate choice to present continuity') had no source and was removed.

era-1795.says: Dirk Langendijk's design in the Rijksmuseum shows the Dutch Maiden and the Lion holding a spear topped with a liberty cap, in the upper-left corner of the existing flag, for the Batavian navy, effective 1 March 1796. FOTW, citing Wilson (1986, p. 60), puts the decree altering the navy's flags (not the merchant flags) on 14 February 1796; the States General publication Wikipedia cites carries the same date.
era-1795.open: The emblem was on the navy's flag only. Its removal in 1806 is Wikipedia's, without a citation. FOTW also describes a tricolour 'with a small white canton' (credited to Roy Stilling, 1996), which we have not reconciled with the Maiden emblem. This page used to describe a 'canton with a liberty cap used briefly 1795-96'; that is not what the sources show.

era-1650.says: Red replaced orange gradually. Wikipedia places the transition between about 1630 and 1660, with red appearing as early as 1596-97 (its infobox and text differ), the name Statenvlag in 1664 (de Jonge, 1833, p. 75) and the navy always flying it after 1663 (de Waard, 1900). The Royal House says red gradually replaced orange during the 17th century because orange is less visible at sea. Wikipedia gives the Republic's distance from the House of Orange as the reason.
era-1650.open: No decree for the change was found, so 'c. 1650' is the midpoint of a transition, not an event. This page used to say the flag flew over the VOC and WIC fleets, New Amsterdam and Batavia; no source for that was found and it was removed.

era-1581.says: Orange-white-blue is attested from the 1570s. Wikipedia cites Rey (1837) for use by the Prince of Orange then, Jacob Duym for officers' brassards at the siege of Leiden in 1574, an order of the Admiralty of Zeeland of 1587 for naval flags in these colours, and de Waard (1900) for the navy flying it from 1588 to 1630. The Royal House dates the first reference to 1572; FOTW says it was used from the second half of the 16th century and named for William of Orange.
era-1581.open: Wikipedia calls it uncertain whether the Sea Beggars carried the colours at Den Briel in 1572, so this page no longer says it flew from the Sea Beggars onward. The era starts at the Act of Abjuration (1581), not at the flag's first appearance. The earliest colour image, of 1575 in Jan van Hout's album, is on Wikipedia without a reference we could read.

era-1433.says: The Cross of Burgundy was the emblem of the Burgundian dukes (Hutchinson, 2007, as cited on Wikipedia). It is drawn here as the emblem, not as a flag of the northern provinces.
era-1433.open: Its use as a flag across the Habsburg Netherlands after 1477 is stated on Wikipedia without a citation and has not been confirmed.

era-1000.says: No single polity existed, so there is no flag to attest; the maroon field is a placeholder.

era-50bce.says: Tacitus (Histories 4.22) describes the force under Civilis following images of wild beasts brought out of woods and sacred groves, and names the Batavian elite and 'German allies'. He describes no flag.
era-50bce.open: This page used to say Tacitus records Batavian and Frisian war-standards; the passage names the Batavians and unnamed German allies, not the Frisii.
